Spatial across ages: 4–5 years · 5–7 years · 7–9 years · 9–12 years · 12–25 years

Mental rotation of objects and scenes

Relative to the 7-year baseline (faster, more reliable object rotation and emerging but still fragile Level-2 perspective taking) nine-year-olds add measurable speed, scale, and compositionality to spatial transformations. From 7-9, performance on mental rotation tasks (including both objects and scenes) continues to sharply increase 1, 2, 3, 4; in the classic (and relatively challenging) Mental Rotation Test (MRT), some studies put 9-years-old as the age when children begin performing above chance levels 5. Beyond improved accuracy, a critical transition toward automatization emerges around age 9: one study demonstrated that motor-mental rotation interference effects present in children younger than 9 years (including 5- and 8-year-olds) disappear around age 9 and in adults 1, suggesting that mental rotation processes become functionally decoupled from concurrent motor activity at this developmental juncture, which is consistent with studies showing that the rate of improvement in object-based mental rotation tasks may begin to decrease towards the end of this window 2, 4. Performance on spatial tasks changes with age in this window. (Figure). Speed of mental rotation improves with age. (Figure).

The rate of improvement in the ability to mentally rotate objects appears to begin slowing down towards the end of this age window, while mental rotation of scenes ("perspective taking") is in the midst of its most rapid improvements 6, 2, 7. Overall, these changes mark age nine as a pivot point where children’s spatial computations begin to resemble a genuinely internalized and flexibly deployable transformation system rather than a motor-anchored skill still in the process of consolidation.

Navigation, path integration, and cognitive mapping

The 7-9 year window marks a critical inflection point in navigation development, defined most saliently by the emergence of proficient cognitive mapping (allocentric spatial representations) and shortcut-taking capabilities that were largely absent at seven. Around age nine, children exhibit a distinct developmental change in their ability to orient and navigate using cognitive maps, demonstrated most clearly by their newfound capacity to identify and use novel shortcuts and detours spontaneously when navigating virtual environments to reach target locations quickly 8, a cardinal signature of true survey knowledge that seven- and eight-year-olds notably lack when tested under identical conditions (performance does, however, remain far from adult-like 9). Starting from age nine, children’s navigational capabilities also expand to encompass large-scale spaces, with metric information being used more frequently and systematically than ever before, and children showing emerging ability to switch between egocentric and allocentric strategies during navigation tasks 10, 11, whereas seven-year-olds remain confined primarily to demonstrating competence in small, simplified environments and continue to default to egocentric strategies even when allocentric approaches (viewpoint-independent localization rather than "this-way-then-that-way") would be more efficient. Fundamentally, the capacity for route integration (mentally relating separately learned routes to form a unified spatial representation) shows significant age-related improvement during this window, with within-route knowledge (knowing locations along a single path) developing more rapidly than between-route knowledge (inferring spatial relations between locations learned via different paths), and the latter showing the strongest gains during this window 12. Overall, the period from 7 to 9 years marks a transition from the piecemeal, route-bound navigation of early childhood to a far more flexible, map-like spatial competence by age nine, characterized by robust allocentric representations, integrated geometric-landmark cues, novel shortcut taking, and greatly enhanced spatial planning and path integration accuracy; performance does, however, remain limited in terms of the rate of errors, the speed of exploration/learning, and in the fusion of self-motion and visual cues 13.
